sources.title: Climate migrants: Dominican Republic: Country Report
sources.temporal_coverage: Climate-migration projections for 2050 and 2100; qualitative case-study interviews in Restauración reported in the 2024 country report.
sources.methodology: Quantitative climate-migration modeling plus qualitative interviews in Restauración.
sources.limitations: Projections are uncertain; interviews reflect one agricultural-border locality, not population prevalence.

sources.title: Dominican Republic Poverty Assessment 2023: Background Note on Poverty and Climate Change
sources.temporal_coverage: Uses a 2021 flood-risk household survey for reported impacts and coping in April 2019–April 2021, plus historical household and hazard data.
sources.methodology: Uses a 2,057-household 2021 flood survey and risk maps.

sources.title: Dominican Republic: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director
sources.temporal_coverage: 2025 Article IV report; reports recent policy and disaster conditions, including Hurricane Fiona in 2022 and climate projections to 2050.
sources.methodology: Article IV report covers climate and disaster-risk policy.
sources.limitations: WB source for some impacts; policy tools not evaluated.

claims.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. ix), Key Messages; PDF pp. 11–12 (printed pp. 3–4), migration patterns
claims.paraphrase: The model projects Haiti-origin climate migrants into Dominican border, farm and urban areas; lagging border infrastructure may heighten competition with host communities over scarce resources.
claims.scenario: RCP2.6/8.5 paired with SSP2/4; projections extend to 2050 and 2100.
affected_groups: host communities in Dominican border areas
claims.limitations: Potential tension, not observed violence; estimates assume no change in border policy or Haiti’s political-economic context.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The report says competition over limited resources may elevate tensions between host and migrant communities.

claims.locator: PDF p. 12 (printed p. 4), Restauración case study, climate and agricultural productivity
claims.paraphrase: Interviewees in Restauración, Dajabón, linked rainfall shifts and land degradation to lower farm yields and migration intentions.
claims.limitations: Employment and education also mattered; interview evidence is qualitative and single-locality.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 12–13 (printed pp. 4–5), Restauración case study and adaptation discussion
claims.paraphrase: Some Restauración farmers diversified into forestry and agroforestry; local association nurseries provided plants, but time, land and investment constrained poorer farmers.
affected_groups: farmers with limited land or investment resources
claims.limitations: Interviewees described examples; report says nursery assistance was not widespread across households.

claims.locator: PDF p. 13 (printed p. 12), urban exposure and FIAS findings following Figure 10
claims.paraphrase: The note cites estimates that informal settlements house 43% of Greater Santo Domingo residents and 70% of Puerto Plata residents.
claims.limitations: Settlement shares are cited from a CCDR concept note, not estimated by this household survey.

claims.locator: PDF p. 13 (printed p. 12), discussion accompanying Figure 11, survey losses 2019–2021
claims.paraphrase: Surveyed household-goods losses associated with floods or excess rainfall in 2019–21 were concentrated mainly in the south and southwest.
affected_groups: households reporting flood or rainfall losses
claims.limitations: Self-reported survey losses; the report gives broad regions here.

claims.locator: PDF p. 15 (printed p. 14), section 4.2.3 and Figure 12, flood risk by wealth and rural/urban location
claims.paraphrase: Poor people were 46% of residents in highly flood-prone areas; one in four households in the bottom two wealth quintiles faced high flood risk.
claims.limitations: Poverty is defined using the survey asset-wealth index.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 22 and 34 (printed pp. 21 and 33), coping analysis and conclusion
claims.paraphrase: The note reports poor households may sell assets, migrate, remove children from school, or cut food, health and education consumption after climate shocks.
claims.limitations: These are coping pathways summarized by the report, not a forecast for every household.

claims.locator: PDF p. 30 (printed p. 29), female-headed household warning and information access
claims.paraphrase: Female-headed households were less likely than male-headed households to receive flood warnings (40% vs 47%) or seek weather information (50% vs 56%).
claims.limitations: 2021 survey; the report notes age may affect information-channel use.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 96–97, Annex I, para. 2, climate trends and projections
claims.paraphrase: IMF reports mean temperature rose 0.73°C since 1950; another 0.63–1.94°C rise and declining precipitation are projected by 2050.
claims.scenario: 2050 projection; cited paragraph omits emissions scenario.
claims.limitations: National aggregate; local variation is not stated.

claims.locator: PDF p. 96, Annex I, para. 2 and footnote 4, Hurricane Fiona impacts
claims.paraphrase: Hurricane Fiona (2022) damaged over 8,500 homes, displaced over 43,000 people and disrupted water for more than one million households.
claims.limitations: IMF cites WB project estimate; no climate attribution.

claims.locator: PDF p. 96, Annex I, para. 2 and footnote 5, water access
claims.paraphrase: Six in ten residents experience intermittent water supply; low-income households may spend up to 12% of income on bottled water.
claims.limitations: National figures; the cited passage gives no subnational breakdown.

claims.locator: PDF p. 99, Annex I, para. 9, climate-responsive social protection
claims.paraphrase: IVACC and FIBE guide Emergency Bonus targeting using structural damage, health effects and income loss after weather emergencies.
claims.limitations: Temporary transfer and targeting tools are described; delivery outcomes are not evaluated.

claims.locator: PDF p. 99, Annex I, para. 10, disaster-risk governance and local committees
claims.paraphrase: Municipal disaster committees prepare local emergency plans, but misaligned plans and weak cross-level coordination hinder unified response.
institutions: municipal Committees for Disaster Prevention, Mitigation, and Response
claims.limitations: IMF describes system-level constraints, not performance in individual municipalities.

search_audit.query: Dominican Republic primary report subnational flood, poverty, informal settlement and climate vulnerability by province/city
search_audit.outcome: Opened World Bank climate-migration and poverty/climate reports; found named Dajabón/Restauración, Greater Santo Domingo and Puerto Plata evidence, plus broad southern/southwestern household losses and wealth- and gender-differentiated exposure.

search_audit.query: Dominican Republic climate migration Haiti border host migrant resource competition tensions World Bank report
search_audit.outcome: The World Bank report explicitly projects potential host–migrant tensions over scarce resources in underdeveloped border areas; it does not document resulting violence.

search_audit.query: Dominican Republic Haiti insecurity conflict violence border disruption climate adaptation emergency response primary report
search_audit.outcome: Reviewed full climate-migration and IMF disaster-governance reports and targeted searches; no opened primary source linked conflict or insecurity to interrupted Dominican climate adaptation. The migration model assumes no change in border policy and Haiti’s political-economic context; no reverse pathway is claimed.

search_audit.query: Dominican Republic disaster risk preparedness municipal committees social protection climate vulnerability index emergency bonus resilience
search_audit.outcome: The IMF report describes climate-sensitive social-protection targeting, local disaster committees and coordination gaps; the World Bank field study documents agroforestry and nursery support in Restauración, while the poverty note reports limited warning reach and costly coping.

gaps: DOM is absent from EXISTING_COUNTRIES.json and no countries/DOM baseline dossier was present; this is a new-country extraction, not an extension of an existing record.

The strongest direct climate–FCV evidence is a modeled, conditional climate-migration pathway with potential host–migrant tension; the reviewed primary sources do not establish observed climate-driven violence in the Dominican Republic.
No reviewed primary source linked insecurity or conflict to interrupted Dominican climate adaptation or disaster response. Not found is not evidence of absence.

The Ministry of Environment adaptation-plan link returned HTTP 500; the IMF Climate Policy Diagnostic formats returned internal errors; the 2025 health adaptation plan was discoverable only through metadata/abstract. Their text is not used.
The World Bank poverty note relies on a 2021 flood-risk survey for 2019–2021 impacts; climate-migration results are scenario-dependent model estimates, not observed forecasts.
